name: Clustering Papers by Meaning
title: Clustering Papers by Meaning
answer: Clustering papers by meaning groups research works according to what they argue or investigate, not just shared keywords or citations. It is used to find thematic families, overlaps between fields, and gaps in a literature. The practice sits inside citation mapping and discovery, where a reader wants to move from one paper to a body of related work. A small working library, such as the 135 papers held on this site, is enough to make meaningful clusters when the papers are chosen around a question.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Clustering papers by meaning groups research works according to what they argue or investigate, not just shared keywords or citations. It is used to find thematic families, overlaps between fields, and gaps in a literature. The practice sits inside citation mapping and discovery, where a reader wants to move from one paper to a body of related work. A small working library, such as the 135 papers held on this site, is enough to make meaningful clusters when the papers are chosen around a question.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on text embeddings produced by transformer language models, which turn titles, abstracts, or full text into fixed-length vectors. These vectors are stored in a vector index that supports fast nearest-neighbour search. Clustering then runs on the similarity scores or on a reduced two-dimensional projection of the vectors. No specialised hardware is required for a few hundred papers; a standard CPU is sufficient for embedding and clustering at that scale.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pipeline embeds each paper's abstract and title, computes pairwise cosine similarity, and applies a density-based or hierarchical clustering algorithm. Cluster labels are then derived from the most frequent terms, key phrases, or extracted claims in each group. When a library has structured claims, as this site does with 11,075 extracted claims, clustering can be run on claim-level embeddings to separate distinct findings within a single paper. The result is a map of meaning rather than a list of keywords.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Clustering by meaning can overstate similarity, hide minority views, or inherit bias from the embedding model's training data. Provenance matters because a cluster is a derived artefact, not a source; every member should link back to the original paper. This site follows that rule by never linking to the Consensus search tool and always linking to the original research work. Rights risk is lower when only abstracts and metadata are embedded; full-text clustering raises access and copyright considerations.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Clustering is moving toward interactive maps where a reader can zoom from a whole field to a single claim and back. Embeddings will increasingly include figures, equations, and citation context, not just words. Cluster explanations are likely to become more faithful, with short natural-language summaries tied to the underlying papers. The goal is discovery that keeps the reader anchored to primary sources while revealing structure across hundreds or thousands of works.
